choices.text: Assign the king room to Elena and her spouse and the queen room to the cousin.
Assign the king room to Elena and her spouse and a twin room to the cousin.
Assign a twin room to Elena and her spouse and the king room to the cousin.
Assign the queen room to Elena and her spouse and the king room to the cousin.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A and D use the same inventory at the same total cost and differ only in which room receives which bed. A recognizes that a king is acceptable in some circumstances but misses both the preference ordering and the requirement to apply it per room rather than across the reservation as a whole.
candidate.gold_action: Assign the queen room to Elena and her spouse and the king room to the cousin.
candidate.label_rationale: The preference applies to Elena and her spouse’s shared room, not to every room in the reservation. Room 1 should receive the queen, while the bed-flexible solo traveler can receive the remaining king room.
candidate.query: On a personal trip to Lisbon, Elena and her spouse will share Room 1, while her adult cousin will occupy Room 2 alone and has stated no bed preference. At the selected hotel, exactly one standard queen room and one standard king room remain, both with the same rate, cancellation terms, floor, and view. Twin rooms are also available on a quieter floor at the same rate. Which allocation should the planner make?

choices.text: Confirm the complimentary king upgrade on the same floor.
Confirm the queen room on the same floor at the booked rate.
Confirm the two-double room with the earlier check-in time.
Move to a nearby queen room with late checkout at the same total price.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A is especially tempting because the history allows a king as a larger alternative and generic loyalty logic favors free upgrades. The item requires recognizing that acceptability does not reverse the ordering when the preferred room remains equally available.
candidate.gold_action: Decline the automatic upgrade and confirm the otherwise identical queen room.
candidate.label_rationale: The history distinguishes the preferred configuration from a larger alternative that is merely acceptable. Because the queen remains available with no offsetting disadvantage, the preferred option should be confirmed rather than treating the word ‘upgrade’ as dispositive.
candidate.query: For a personal stay in Copenhagen, Elena and her spouse are sharing one room. The hotel has preassigned a complimentary king upgrade, but an otherwise identical queen room on the same floor is still available at the booked rate. Accepting or declining the upgrade changes no benefits, status credit, cancellation terms, or check-in time. Two-double inventory with early check-in is also available. What should the planner confirm?

choices.text: Assign the standard king room to Elena and her spouse, and assign the standard queen room to the cousin.
Assign the standard king room to Elena and her spouse, and assign a standard twin room to the cousin.
Assign a standard twin room to Elena and her spouse, and assign the standard king room to the cousin.
Assign the standard queen room to Elena and her spouse, and assign the standard king room to the cousin.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A and D consume exactly the same queen and king inventory and are identical on rate, terms, room quality, and convenience. Only Elena's longitudinal, room-specific preference determines which traveler should receive the queen, while the acceptability of a king makes A a plausible near miss.
candidate.gold_action: Assign the standard queen room to Elena and her spouse and the standard king room to the bed-flexible cousin.
candidate.label_rationale: Across three separate trips, Elena established that the bed policy applies specifically to the room she shares with her spouse: a queen is preferred, a king is an acceptable larger fallback, and separate beds should be used only when explicitly requested. Because the cousin has no bed preference and all generic room attributes are equal, the queen should be allocated to Elena and her spouse and the remaining king to the cousin.
candidate.query: For a personal trip to Lisbon, Elena and her spouse will share Room 1, while her adult cousin will occupy Room 2 alone and has stated no bed preference. The selected hotel has exactly one standard queen room, one standard king room, and several standard twin rooms available. All are on the same floor and have the same rate, cancellation terms, view category, room size, and check-in availability. Which allocation should the planner make?

query_only_verdict.rationale: The king room is the best standard fit for the two adults sharing Room 1. For the cousin occupying Room 2 alone, the queen room weakly dominates a twin room at the same rate and under otherwise identical conditions. Choices C and D allocate the uniquely larger king bed to the solo traveler while giving the couple a smaller or less suitable arrangement.
